body: Monday, July 27 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed is expected to hold rates steady this week, but a rate hike is genuinely on the table for the first time in this cycle — oil-driven inflation resurgence has turned the July FOMC into what the press is calling a "rate-hike showdown." Fiscal stance remains expansionary with Trump talking up the economy ahead of Michigan congressional races. The 10Y yield is surging at 4.64% (+27 bps vs 4W), the 2Y at 4.33% (prior close, +24 bps vs 4W), and the curve is positively sloped at +36bps but still flat by historical standards — a mild bear steepener driven by hawkish repricing across the curve on inflation fears, not by easing expectations. S&P 500 at 7387 is marginally positive (↑0.4%) but the Nasdaq 100 is sharply underperforming (↓5.3%), signaling a dramatic rotation away from growth/duration-sensitive assets.

New / Most Important: The US-Iran conflict paused — the US halted attacks on Iran, sending oil prices down ~5% on the day and WTI to a one-week low. However, oil remains massively elevated at 82.85 (↑19.7% vs 4W). The IMF warned that all three oil market "shock absorbers" have been depleted, meaning any resumption of hostilities flows directly into prices. This week's Fed decision and Big Tech earnings (Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon) represent a binary event cluster that will define Q3 positioning. Dollar funding stress and FX liquidity risk are flagged as active concerns for S&P 500 fragility.

Playbook ✓: Oil shock → inflation fears → hawkish Fed repricing → growth-to-value rotation → curve steepening. This is textbook commodity-shock transmission.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The S&P 500 sitting near highs while Nasdaq craters 5.3% is structurally unusual — it implies massive inflows into energy, industrials, and defensives are offsetting the tech drawdown. This is NOT the 2022 playbook where everything fell together. What's happening is a capital flow rotation within equities that keeps index-level volatility suppressed (VIX only 19.5) while sector-level dislocations are enormous. The growth pulse shows the market is pricing BOTH a supply shock AND real economic activity — July flash PMIs are expanding (US manufacturing at 53.8, euro-zone activity back in growth for the first time in four months) even as oil surges — an unusual dual signal that typically resolves violently in one direction. If the Fed actually hikes, the "soft landing while hiking into a war" narrative would be unprecedented and deeply fragile. The Russell/Nasdaq ratio rising 3.3% confirms breadth is expanding into small-caps, but the Russell itself is down 2.2% in absolute terms — so this is a "less bad" rotation, not a genuine broadening.

Macro Stance: The ECB held rates at 2.25% on July 23, explicitly citing the reignited Iran conflict and its inflation implications. The easing cycle that had been underway is now frozen. ECB's Kazimir stated publicly that "one more interest rate hike is needed," marking a hawkish pivot in the Governing Council's rhetoric. The bank lending survey from July 21 will be the key data point for assessing credit transmission.

New / Most Important: The ECB's hold was widely expected, but the door being kept "open to further rate hikes" is a material shift. This is structurally new: the ECB was in an easing cycle as recently as Q1 2026, and the pivot to considering hikes represents the fastest monetary policy whipsaw in ECB history. Europe's energy vulnerability is orders of magnitude higher than the US — Brent-linked gas contracts and the EU's still-incomplete energy diversification from Russian supply mean any sustained oil shock transmits into headline and core inflation simultaneously. The September hike pricing in markets is a scenario most European equity investors have not hedged for. UK defence spending expansion (per Blain's Morning Porridge) adds a fiscal impulse that complicates the ECB's calculus for eurozone-adjacent economies.

Playbook ✓: Energy shock → ECB hawkish hold → euro supported vs. dollar — classic.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The speed of the pivot from easing to potential hiking is the divergence. Markets had priced terminal rate cuts through 2026; that entire forward curve is now being repriced. European credit spreads should be widening more aggressively than they appear to be, suggesting either complacency or stealth central bank intervention in peripheral spreads.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is easing through volume, not price. Loan prime rates were left unchanged for a 14th consecutive month (The Business Times, [Jul 20]), even with growth below target. Instead the central bank added the most liquidity in five months (Bloomberg, [Jul 23]) and is running overnight reverse repos alongside a 500b-yuan MLF operation, injecting a total of 2.1 trillion yuan (Reuters, [Jul 24]; China Daily, [Jul 24]). The yuan is not the release valve: UOB sees an upside bias against the dollar below 6.7820 (www.tmgm.com, [Jul 20]) as Europe scrutinises its value (Bloomberg, [Jul 21]). Prices are split: June CPI rose only 1% (Global Times, [Jul 9]) while PPI climbed 4.1% (finance.biggo.com, [Jul 8]), a near four-year high that squeezes manufacturers (Reuters, [Jul 8]).

PMIs & Activity: The last official read is June: manufacturing PMI 50.3 and non-manufacturing 50.2 (Reuters, [Jun 29]); July's numbers are the next test (ING Think, [Jul 23]). The hard data show two speeds: Q2 GDP grew 4.3%, below the official target range (Bloomberg, [Jul 15]); June industrial output rose 5.3% y/y and retail sales returned to growth (BusinessLine, [Jul 15]), but first-half retail sales were up just 1.3% (Ecns.cn, [Jul 15]) and the investment slide deepened as infrastructure joined property (Caixin Global, [Jul 15]), while June exports surged 27% from a year earlier (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 13]). Now the factory engine is slowing too: industrial profit growth slowed again in June as retreating oil prices sapped the earnings lift (CNBC, [Jul 26]), to the slowest pace this year (Financial Times, [Jul 26]). Trade-in sales are dropping as the stimulus effect fades (Caixin Global, [Jul 24]).

Credit Impulse: June new bank loans rose less than expected (The Star, [Jul 15]) and credit growth missed as the PBOC flagged a "new normal" (Caixin Global, [Jul 16]). Household loans fell by 366.8 billion yuan in the first half (36Kr, [Jul 17]). The finance minister's claim that fiscal-financial synergy leveraged over 17 trillion yuan in new loans (finance.biggo.com, [Jul 22]) is not a contradiction: the volume is policy-directed corporate and state-linked lending while households pay down, and NST Online argues the real challenge is household confidence rather than property ([Jul 26]). Banks breaking with the lending benchmark in pricing new credit (Bloomberg, [Jul 24]) is quiet price easing. Read: headline impulse flat, household impulse negative.

Property: June new home prices fell at a slower pace (Reuters, [Jul 14]) and first-tier prices extended a four-month rebound (South China Morning Post, [Jul 15]), but resale prices fell faster (Reuters, [Jun 30]) and property investment slumped 18 percent y/y in January–June (The Standard (HK), [Jul 15]). The capital side is in retreat: KKR and AEW seek to sell China assets at steep losses (Bloomberg, [Jul 20]), and regulators curbed a loan structure used by distressed developers (Bloomberg, [Jul 22]) and offshore loans for local real estate firms (The Standard (HK), [Jul 23]). Vanke completed extensions on its 2026 public bonds (Caixin Global, [Jul 23]) with a RMB 519 million loan from Shenzhen Metro at 2.29% (BigGo Finance, [Jul 21]): state shareholders, not buyers, hold it together.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing pledged stronger policy support (TradingView, [Jul 21]) and vowed to hit the growth target (Bloomberg, [Jul 20]), yet clings to austerity despite the slowdown (Bloomberg, [Jul 22]), and growth is set to slow in the second half as it avoids broad stimulus (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 25]). The July Politburo meeting, still ahead, is the marker for the growth commitment (Bloomberg, [Jul 23]). Regulation is tightening at the edges: Trip.com was fined US$765 million in an antitrust action (PYMNTS.com, [Jul 26]). On trade, Washington will impose new tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on over 60 countries (China Daily Global Edition, [Jul 24]); Beijing is set to look past them before Xi's US trip (Bloomberg, [Jul 24]) and is consulting on tariff cuts on $30 billion in trade (Reuters, [Jul 23]). Toward Europe it keeps adding EU companies to its dual-use export control list (Table.Briefings, [Jul 26]).

Markets & Flows: Capital is chasing AI, not consumption. CXMT's 466% debut surge made it the most valuable China-listed company (CNBC, [Jul 26]) and revived interest in battered shares (TradingView, [Jul 26]), after the "national team" bought shares worth $9bn (Financial Times, [Jul 20]). Hong Kong is weaker: it sank back below 25,000 on oil and tariff fears (BusinessToday Malaysia, [Jul 25]) as Middle East tensions weighed on the week (BusinessToday Malaysia, [Jul 26]). BCA tips a three-month reversion trade into China away from South Korea (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 25]). ASML's slide on China-related news shows how fast export-control risk now hits Western equipment makers.

New / Most Important: June industrial profits remove the last cushion in the domestic story. First-half profits rose 18.7% (TradingView, [Jul 26]), but growth is now the slowest this year, and Reuters frames exports as what cushions an uneven recovery ([Jul 26]). With retail demand soft, household credit shrinking and the budget on austerity, the oil-price lift to margins was the bridge; it is fading ahead of a July Politburo meeting that must decide whether fiscal policy finally steps in.

Playbook ✓: Stimulus drip-feed, weak property, LPR on hold and export-led profits are all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Markets are bidding China's AI champions while the growth pulse weakens underneath: slower profits, an 18 percent property-investment slump and contracting infrastructure keep construction-linked bulk demand fading, a drag on iron ore and on the AUD, whose bounce as Mideast tensions ease rests on oil, not China. European exporters absorb the surplus as the yuan draws scrutiny, and EM inflows ride state buying and IPO euphoria rather than a PMI or credit upturn. A turn needs household credit and fiscal transfers, not liquidity alone.

Macro Stance: The BOJ is signaling more rate hikes as price pressures build. The yen remains near multi-decade lows (~160 per dollar), and the weak yen combined with high oil prices is creating an imported inflation spiral. The BOJ is now said to be "open to a faster rate hike pace," with markets pricing a move to 1.25% and a potential hike by October or December per Reuters polling. A "giant spending spree" by the PM is raising Liz Truss comparisons in global media.

New / Most Important: This is structurally significant and warrants extended treatment. Japan is simultaneously running the most aggressive fiscal expansion in decades while its central bank accelerates tightening — a direct policy contradiction that mirrors the UK's 2022 gilts crisis. The weak yen is no longer a competitiveness boost; at these levels with oil at $83, it is an inflation accelerant that forces the BOJ's hand. The carry trade unwind risk is enormous: if BOJ hikes faster than expected while the Fed holds or hikes (compressing the rate differential less than hoped), yen shorts may not unwind — trapping carry traders in a scenario where they're paying more to borrow yen but not getting yen appreciation. The Nikkei is rising per the feed, but this may be the last gasp of the weak-yen export earnings boost before BOJ tightening crushes domestic credit. The fiscal-monetary conflict is the single most dangerous macro setup globally right now. If JGB yields spike on fiscal concerns (Truss analogy), the BOJ's YCC successor framework will be tested in ways that could cascade into global bond markets.

Playbook ✓: Weak yen → BOJ hike expectations → yen carry unwind fears — all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The fiscal blowout is the divergence. The BOJ cannot credibly tighten monetary policy while the government floods the economy with spending. This is the tension that broke the UK in 2022, and the scale of Japan's debt-to-GDP makes the stakes exponentially higher.

Macro Stance: The RBA is now "twice as likely to hike" according to The Guardian, with traders "convinced" a fourth rate rise is coming after a jobs surge. Petrol prices threatening A$2/litre add consumer pressure. The RBA's own community survey revealed Australians broadly misunderstand how interest rates work — a political constraint on further tightening.

New / Most Important: The AUD is gaining as Mideast tensions ease, but the domestic picture is stagflationary: strong labour market forcing the RBA to consider hiking into a consumer already squeezed by elevated mortgage rates. The commodity terms-of-trade boost partially offsets the oil import drag, though iron ore rests on Chinese construction, where property investment slumped 18 percent y/y in January–June.  |  Playbook ✓: Commodity-linked FX + hawkish RBA = AUD supported.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The SMH editorial arguing "more hikes aren't the solution" signals political pushback is building. If the RBA hikes again, it risks becoming the poster child for overtightening into a housing-leveraged economy.

Macro Stance: The RPP is drifting hawkish while the data run hot. Kotecki said the inflation picture is diverging from the NBP projection and it is too early to talk about a September cut (pb.pl, [Jul 23]); another Council hawk called the earlier cuts premature (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 21]) and one member said hikes are now more likely than cuts (Super Biznes, [Jul 21]). The dovish side is thinner: Crédit Agricole still expects a 25 bp cut in September to 3.50% as the terminal level (PAP Biznes, [Jul 20]), but CEO Magazyn warned the oil shock could stop Polish cuts altogether [Jul 23]. Inflation itself looks tame: it fell to 3% (Obserwator Gospodarczy, [Jul 22]) and Poland slid to 17th in the EU inflation table (INNPoland.pl, [Jul 27]). Activity is the doves' problem: June retail sales rose 6.2% y/y in constant prices against a 5.2% consensus (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 22]), industrial production rose 7.6% (CEO Magazyn, [Jul 20]) and ING BSK sees roughly 3.8% y/y GDP growth in Q2 (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 22]). Wages rose 5.9% y/y in June with employment falling (StockWatch.pl, [Jul 20]), unemployment fell (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 23]) and producer prices rose for a fourth month (CEO Magazyn, [Jul 20]).

Markets: Warsaw is pressing on a record with one casualty. Parkiet had the WIG20 aiming at a record going into the week [Jul 27] after the index stalled at the 3900 mark (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 23]). On Monday Żabka fell 12.5% early (Strefa Inwestorów, [Jul 27]) and ended down around 14% after Seven & i walked away from stake talks (Briefs Finance, [Jul 27]), while Dino and CD Projekt led the gainers and the main indices closed higher (Inwestycje.pl, [Jul 27]). Orlen keeps breaking records with analysts lifting targets (Comparic.pl, [Jul 27]); PGE jumped 7.37% on Jul 23 as banks sank (FXMAG), and KGHM lost 3.97% on Friday (FXMAG, [Jul 24]). The card confirms the energy tilt: Orlen at 156.0 is up 6.7% on the week and 26.4% over four weeks, PGE at 10.48 is up 10.5% and 9.2%, Allegro at 44.74 is up 20.3% in four weeks; KGHM at 303.5 is still down 7.4% over four weeks, Dino (-1.3% 1W) and CD Projekt (-2.6% 1W) lagged, PKO was flat at -0.2% and Pekao rose 2.1%. EPOL closed at 40.92, up 1.4% on the week and 6.1% over four weeks. The zloty is firmer: USD/PLN closed at 3.7864 (-0.3% 1W, +0.6% 4W) and EUR/PLN at 4.3147 (-0.6% 1W, +0.7% 4W), with MyBank.pl putting EUR/PLN near 4.31 as the dollar weakened [Jul 27]. The weak leg is debt: yields jumped sharply even as the euro stayed stable (Bankier.pl, [Jul 24]) and the August retail bond offer was left unchanged (Business Insider Polska, [Jul 27]).

Fiscal & Politics: The debt story turned loud. Public debt reached 61.6% of GDP, the third fastest increase in the EU (XYZ, [Jul 21]), Treasury debt exceeds 2.1 trillion zł (Do Rzeczy, [Jul 24]), it has climbed above 500 billion euros at a record borrowing pace (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]) and Arak expects more than 70% of GDP by end-2027 (Filary Biznesu, [Jul 26]). Policy pulls the other way: the finance ministry has advanced variants of a 60 000 zł tax-free allowance (Polskie Radio 24, [Jul 24]), PIT changes could leave up to 433 zł more in pockets (Fakt, [Jul 27]) and the ministry withdrew planned lump-sum tax increases (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 27]). On the revenue side the Sejm passed a savings tax from 2027 (Gazeta Prawna, [Jul 25]) and the digital tax drew a US retaliation threat (Briefs Finance, [Jul 22]). The sharpest clash is fuel: President Nawrocki sent the windfall-profits tax to the Constitutional Tribunal, freezing 4 billion zł of CPN programme funding (Gov.pl, [Jul 27]), the government is redesigning the fuel levy on the bank-tax model (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 27]) and Bloomberg reported Poland may revive fuel-price caps [Jul 27] as diesel threatens 8 zł (Rzeczpospolita, [Jul 27]).

Corporate & Sectors: Allegro named Katarzyna Ostap-Tomann of Cyfrowy Polsat as CFO after Jonathan Eastick resigned (Parkiet, [Jul 27]). PGE GiEK extended the oldest coal units at Rybnik to 2028 with a gas plant to follow (Dziennik Zachodni, [Jul 27]). Orlen flagged lower crude throughput and impairments in its Q2 estimates (Energetyka24.com, [Jul 22]). CD Projekt will show the Witcher 3 expansion at gamescom (pb.pl, [Jul 21]) with the stock around 230 zł (Comparic.pl, [Jul 21]). Banks face the CHF law from early August with instalments suspended by statute (Franknews.pl, [Jul 25]), yet pb.pl argued debt and credit could lift bank profits by up to half by 2030 [Jul 27]. Dino overtook Eurocash in grocery (Wiadomości Handlowe, [Jul 27]); Warsaw flat prices are falling (Subiektywnie o finansach, [Jul 22]) and rental listings dropped 3.2% m/m in June (PAP Biznes, [Jul 22]).

Geopolitics & Security: Belarus moved special forces to the Ukrainian border (TVP Info, [Jul 22]) and troops are reported on the Polish border itself (Kresy24.pl, [Jul 23]); Warsaw warned Russia may turn captured Ukrainian drones against Poland and the Baltics (Defense News, [Jul 21]), and NATO's top general said Russia could move on Poland or the Baltics (National Security Journal, [Jul 20]). Poland launched a 205 million dollar defence innovation programme (Anadolu, [Jul 23]), MON will deploy a Smart Border (INNPoland.pl, [Jul 25]) and Poland is bidding for a Patriot factory (Tech Times, [Jul 24]).

New / Most Important: Seven & i dropping Żabka is the week's signal: a 14% hit to a WIG20 name on the day the index was reaching for a record shows how much of the rally rests on takeover premia and foreign bids rather than on domestic fundamentals, which are now fiscal (debt past 60% of GDP) and hawkish (Kotecki). Add the presidential block on the windfall tax and the market is pricing an Orlen that keeps its profits while the budget loses 4 billion zł.  |  Playbook ✓: Stay with the hold call; favour the energy names the card already rewards over bid-dependent consumer stocks, and keep duration short while yields make multi-year highs.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Equities a step from a record against bonds at yield highs and debt at 61.6% of GDP; retail sales at 6.2% against a Council member calling hikes more likely than cuts.

Macro Stance: Brazil's central bank is signaling caution on inflation, consistent with oil pass-through into a still-hot domestic economy. Vietnam is flagged by Vietnam Holding as offering "compelling value" in a resilient economy — this is a supply-chain re-routing beneficiary.  |  Playbook ✓: EM central banks holding or tightening in sympathy with DM hawkishness.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Korea's Hana Securities opening stock market access to foreign investors via Futu is a structural change in EM market microstructure — increased foreign retail access to Korean equities could drive flows into Samsung/SK Hynix as a semi proxy when ASML and Western names face China headwinds.

Narrative: The Nasdaq 100 is down 5.3% vs 4W — its sharpest underperformance against the S&P this cycle — as a 10Y at 4.64% (+27 bps) crushes long-duration multiples; Apple, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon report this week in a pivotal moment for the AI trade.

Reported: IBM cut its annual revenue growth forecast as customers prioritize AI infrastructure spending (Reuters, [Jul 22]), with mainframe sales down 42% (MLQ.ai, [Jul 23]). ServiceNow raised its annual subscription revenue forecast again on AI-driven demand (Reuters, [Jul 22]). SAP jumped as its earnings beat eased AI fears (Barron's, [Jul 24]), even as it lowered operating profit guidance (WSJ, [Jul 23]).

EPS Upside Watch: Oracle — landed a $7 billion Pentagon software contract (TIKR.com, [Jul 24]), contracted revenue still to flow through earnings. Dell — raised guidance by $27 billion and the Street is still catching up (TIKR.com, [Jul 21]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The Nasdaq cratering while the S&P holds near highs breaks the 2023-2025 regime in which mega-cap tech was the market. The AI narrative is not dead, but its equity expression is migrating from pure-play compute to infrastructure, energy and real-economy applications; a Big Tech disappointment could push the drawdown past 10%.
Narrative: Meta's earnings this week are the sector catalyst; consumer engagement stays strong, as YouTube Premium shows, but duration sensitivity drags XLC alongside broader tech.

Reported: Alphabet beat Q2 revenue estimates but dropped 5% on a $205B capex outlook (MLQ.ai, [Jul 23]). Verizon rose on an earnings beat and raised guidance (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 24]). Charter beat estimates, but its subscriber losses suggest a bleak future for cable (Barron's, [Jul 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: Meta — Deutsche Bank expects strong earnings as AI tools boost advertiser returns (TIKR.com, [Jul 26]), the ad-pricing lever behind an EPS surprise.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Big Tech earnings are slamming into a market in revolt over AI spending (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 26]): a revenue beat no longer protects a platform stock, so capex discipline, not growth, is what the market will reward this week.
Narrative: A +36 bps 10Y-2Y curve, 5 bps wider than four weeks ago, is a thin but improving NIM tailwind, and long-end rates with a hawkish Fed underpin bank earnings power.

Reported: Capital One topped earnings estimates as credit losses fell and the Discover integration progressed (Quartz, [Jul 21]). BNP Paribas lifted its dividend as revenue and profit beat (WSJ, [Jul 23]). American Express raised its revenue forecast (Quartz, [Jul 24]) yet sank 6% after its Q2 beat (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 24]).

EPS Upside Watch: Visa — its Q3 report is flagged as a potential catalyst (TradingView, [Jul 23]), with card spending running hot. Robinhood — Bernstein lifted its target to $160 and sees prediction-markets revenue overtaking crypto (The Block, [Jul 20]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The curve is steepening and bank stocks are not pricing recession — they are pricing an inflationary boom, good for earnings but bad for credit books. Commercial real estate exposure is the weak link to watch.

Narrative: WTI at 82.85 (↑19.7% vs 4W) stays the dominant macro story even after the US-Iran pause knocked prices lower on the day, and the IMF warns all three shock absorbers are depleted. With China's industrial profit growth at its slowest this year, this is a supply shock, not demand-led strength.

Reported: TotalEnergies posted its strongest profit in nearly three years on the Iran war (Reuters, [Jul 23]), though lower volumes left it short of estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 24]). SLB gained 11% on a strong beat and a return to revenue growth (TIKR.com, [Jul 26]). Equinor's profits doubled to $11.5bn (The Guardian, [Jul 22]).

EPS Upside Watch: US majors — Big Oil is set to reap a profit bonanza from soaring fuel prices (Bloomberg.com, [Jul 22]). Chevron — screened as poised to beat Q2 earnings estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 20]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Oil falling 5% intraday on the Iran pause while still up about 20% in four weeks shows the market pricing geopolitics as a binary toggle, not a structural supply premium. If the pause is temporary, the snapback will be violent, and low-beta midstream may outperform headline-driven E&Ps.
Narrative: Defence spending is the structural bid, with UK defence investment adding to global rearmament, and AI data-centre and grid build-outs support power and infrastructure-linked industrials.

Reported: RTX raised its guidance three times over in its Q2 report (TIKR.com, [Jul 24]), and Lockheed Martin soared on a beat and a raised full-year guide (ChartMill, [Jul 23]). CSX jumped after robust intermodal demand drove a Q2 beat (TIKR.com, [Jul 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: GE Vernova — Guggenheim raised its target to $1,450 on the beat (Investing.com, [Jul 23]), with data-centre power orders the driver. Vertiv — raised guidance twice this year and the Street is still behind (TIKR.com, [Jul 21]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Inside the S&P 500 AI boom, industrials are getting as rich as tech stocks (CNBC, [Jul 26]): the AI-power names now carry tech-like multiples, and with them tech-like downside if hyperscaler capex is questioned.

Narrative: Options positioning shows a bleak outlook for Tesla, Cracker Barrel's CEO departure signals turnaround failure, and a 52-year-old restaurant chain closing all locations points to accelerating distress as energy costs squeeze consumers.

Reported: Tesla's revenue beat but EPS missed (scanx.trade, [Jul 26]), and the stock plummeted 14% (Forbes, [Jul 23]). General Motors' Q2 beat on every line (TIKR.com, [Jul 22]). Deckers beat and raised guidance, but the shares slid 3.5% (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Ford — looks overlooked ahead of its July 28 Q2 report (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 25]), after upgrades on its profit and cash-flow outlook.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Legacy restaurant chains collapsing while stocks power to new highs exposes a K-shaped consumer: high-income households drive S&P earnings, while the low- and middle-income diners who eat at Cracker Barrel retrench — a divergence the oil shock is widening.
Narrative: Defensive positioning is in vogue as tech sells off, so staples benefit from the rotation out of growth, but elevated energy prices keep input costs under pressure.

Reported: Philip Morris beat as organic sales rose 7.6% (Yahoo Finance, [Jul 22]). Albertsons surprised with Q2 sales, but the stock dropped 14.4% (StockStory, [Jul 23]). Lamb Weston beat expectations in a strong Q2 (StockStory, [Jul 24]).

EPS Upside Watch: Coca-Cola — reports July 28, with the bull case laid out ahead of the print (24/7 Wall St., [Jul 25]). Campbell's — flagged as offering promising upside despite past challenges, a restructuring story inside a defensive sector.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Albertsons is fighting to keep lower-income shoppers from defecting to discounters (Grocery Dive, [Jul 24]) and General Mills faces changing American shoppers (Star Tribune, [Jul 26]): the staples shelter is cracking on volume, not just cost.
Narrative: A politically charged healthcare news cycle adds headline risk, but the sector benefits from the growth-to-defensives rotation.

Reported: UnitedHealth raised its full-year earnings guidance (Investors' Chronicle, [Jul 20]). Thermo Fisher smashed estimates and raised its 2026 outlook as a pharma spending surge lifted growth to 10% (finance.biggo.com, [Jul 23]). Molina beat estimates but is confronting investor doubts (Barron's, [Jul 22]).
EPS Upside Watch: Quest Diagnostics — raised its revenue and EPS guidance for full-year 2026 (PR Newswire, [Jul 23]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Medtech is being sold despite beats — Edwards reversed after its quarterly beat (Investor's Business Daily, [Jul 24]) — so the defensive label is not protecting multiples, even as the slammed group is called a bargain (Barron's, [Jul 24]).
Narrative: Copper at 6.38 (↑3.8%), an AI data-centre and grid-capex metal, and gold at 4083 support materials, with precious-metals miners catching retail attention as gold holds above $4000.

Reported: Freeport-McMoRan beat estimates on rising prices for copper, the grid and data-centre metal (Barron's, [Jul 23]). Dow swung to a profit on higher prices as sales grew (WSJ, [Jul 23]). BASF raised its full-year 2026 earnings outlook after a strong Q2 (European Coatings, [Jul 22]).

EPS Upside Watch: Anglo American — cut its copper cost guidance sharply (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jul 23]), widening margins on a metal priced for AI data-centre and grid build-outs. Gold miners — set for earnings growth, though higher costs could temper gains (Reuters, [Jul 22]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold at 4083 is only ↑0.1% vs 4W, consolidating rather than surging despite a war and rising inflation: the geopolitical premium looks priced, and it needs a new catalyst — a Fed hike or dollar weakness — to break higher.
Narrative: A 10Y at 4.64% (+27 bps vs 4W) is unambiguously negative for rate-sensitive REITs; securitization markets still function, but at wider spreads.
